echo can accept multiple comma-separated arguments and prints them concatenated together, so 'a' followed by 'b' produces 'ab'.
In PHP, print is a language construct that returns 1, making it usable inside expressions (unlike echo which returns no value).
The elvis operator (?:) returns its left operand when it is truthy, not falsy.
In PHP 8, the concatenation operator (.) was given the same precedence as addition and subtraction, not lower precedence.

str_contains returns true because 'Hello world' contains the substring 'world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right (STR_PAD_RIGHT), left (STR_PAD_LEFT), or both sides (STR_PAD_BOTH), not just the right side.
By default, trim() strips all whitespace characters including spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen() returns the number of bytes; 'é' is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so the total is 1+2+1+1+1=6.
When the start position is negative, substr counts from the end of the string, so -3 starts at the 3rd character from the end, returning 'def'.
In PHP, strings are value types and ucfirst() returns a new string without modifying the original variable in place.
Heredoc allows variable interpolation while nowdoc does not, as nowdoc behaves like a single-quoted string.

When array_filter() is called without a callback, it uses a default filtering mechanism that removes all values that evaluate to FALSE in a boolean context (e.g., 0, '', null, false, etc.).
array_slice() re-indexes numeric keys by default (preserve_keys is false), so original numeric keys are not preserved unless you pass true for the fourth parameter.
array_slice with offset 1 and length 2 returns the elements at indices 1 and 2, which are 20 and 30.
The + operator on arrays performs a union by keys, keeping the left operand's value for duplicate keys, resulting in ['a'=>1, 'b'=>2] which has 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 introduced support for string keys in the array spread operator, which previously only worked with integer-keyed arrays.
Named arguments CAN be combined with argument unpacking (...$args) in a single call since PHP 8.0, e.g. foo(...$args, name: 'value') works fine.
In PHP, anonymous functions do not automatically capture variables from the outer scope; variables must be explicitly imported using the `use` keyword.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function, regardless of the declared parameters.
PHP arrow functions (fn) can only have a single expression as their body; you cannot use curly braces with multiple expressions.
PHP arrow functions (fn) capture outer variables by value at definition time, not by reference at use time.
Declaring a closure as `static` in PHP prevents the automatic binding of `$this` to the closure.
The closure captures $x by value (via `use ($x)` without `&`), so it holds 5 at creation time; the later assignment $x = 7 does not affect the captured value.
In weak typing mode (the default), PHP performs type coercion, so passing the numeric string "5" to an int parameter is automatically converted to integer 5.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility modifiers directly on constructor parameters to declare and assign properties in one step.
The 'final' keyword in PHP prevents a method from being overridden in subclasses.
The `final` keyword in PHP explicitly prevents a method from being overridden by any subclass.
Private properties are only accessible within the class that declares them, not in subclasses (that's what `protected` is for).
get_class() on an anonymous class returns 'class@anonymous' followed by a NUL byte and then the file path/line number.
In PHP, private methods are not inherited and are not part of the inheritance contract, so a child class can freely declare a method with the same name with any visibility without conflict.
__get() is also called when accessing inaccessible (private or protected) properties from outside the class scope, not just non-existent properties.
Reassigning a readonly property throws an Error (\Error), not an Exception.
PHP interfaces can declare constants using the `const` keyword, and classes that implement the interface inherit those constants.
The `instanceof` operator in PHP checks whether an object is an instance of a specified class or interface.
PHP interfaces can declare static methods since PHP 5.1.0, and implementing classes must provide those static methods.
The instanceof operator in PHP checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so it does NOT ignore interfaces.
PHP interface methods are always abstract and cannot contain a body/default implementation, unlike trait methods which can provide concrete implementations.
In PHP, abstract methods can have public or protected visibility (and the implementing subclass must match or widen the visibility).
Foo::cases() returns an array of all enum cases, which for this enum with case A, case B, and case C is 3 elements.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants.
In PHP 7+, Throwable is the base interface that both Exception and Error implement, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error, not Exception; both Error and Exception implement Throwable but neither inherits from the other, so catch(Exception) will not catch TypeError.
The @ operator suppresses error messages (warnings, notices, etc.) but does not suppress or catch exceptions.
intdiv() throws a DivisionByZeroError when the divisor is zero.
The finally block always executes regardless of whether an exception was thrown, caught, or even if no exception occurred at all.
An exception thrown inside a finally block overrides the try block's result (return value or exception), so it does have an effect.
In PHP, casting any object to bool always returns true, as objects are always truthy.
Shutdown functions registered via register_shutdown_function() are executed when the script terminates, including when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement only registers an alias for the fully qualified class name; it does not load the file — autoloading occurs when the class is actually referenced in code.
In PHP, 'use function' is the syntax to import a function from a namespace, while 'use const' is for importing constants.
PSR-4 maps the prefix App\ to src/, so the remaining namespace parts Controller\Api\UserController become the sub-path Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php uses spl_autoload_register() to register its class autoloading functions.
__NAMESPACE__ is a PHP magic constant that returns the name of the current namespace as a string, or an empty string if no namespace is defined.
In PHP, an unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace, not from the global root; only fully qualified names (with a leading `\`) resolve from the global root.
PSR-4 maps the prefix 'App\' to 'src/', so removing the prefix from 'App\Model\User' gives 'Model\User', which becomes the path 'src/Model/User.php'.
In PHP, `use` statements for importing namespaces/classes can only appear at the file's top-level or within a namespace declaration; placing them inside a function body results in a parse error.
In PHP, arrays are copied by value on assignment, so modifying one copy does not affect the original.
In PHP, arrays are assigned by value, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
In PHP, functions have their own local scope, so global variables are not accessible inside them without using the `global` keyword, `$GLOBALS`, or being passed as parameters.
$GLOBALS is a superglobal array, so calling unset($GLOBALS['x']) inside a function removes the global variable $x from the global scope for all scripts, not just for that function.
The function takes $x by reference, so $x++ modifies $n directly, making it 6 before echo prints it.
A foreach over an array by value iterates over a copy (snapshot) of the array taken at the start of the loop, so changes to the array inside the loop are not visible in the same pass.
A static property belongs to the class itself and is shared across all instances, so changes in one object are visible in others.
PHP only supports integer and string array keys, so a boolean `true` key is cast to the integer `1`.
Since PHP 7.0, a generator can return a value, and that value is accessible via the getReturn() method on the Generator object after the generator has finished iterating.
In PHP, generators cannot be rewound once they have started yielding; calling rewind() throws an exception.
The `yield from` construct in PHP allows a generator to delegate its traversal to another generator or iterable, yielding all of its values.
A function containing yield is a generator function; calling it returns a Generator object, and get_class() returns its class name 'Generator'.
The generator yields 1, 2, 3; iterator_to_array converts it to an array of 3 elements; count returns 3.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last In, First Out) stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the class that implements a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator is an SPL class that implements Iterator (and other interfaces), wrapping an array to enable traversal using the Iterator interface methods.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate and Iterator, so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates a cryptographically secure salt internally for algorithms like PASSWORD_DEFAULT, PASSWORD_BCRYPT, and PASSWORD_ARGON2ID, so no separate salt is needed.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT is not md5; in PHP 8 it uses Argon2id (and previously bcrypt in earlier PHP versions).
password_verify returns true (boolean) because the same plaintext 'secret' is verified against its own hash generated by password_hash.
strip_tags() only removes HTML and PHP tags from a string and has no relation to SQL injection prevention; use prepared statements or parameterized queries instead.
session_regenerate_id() generates a new session ID after login, invalidating the old one, which prevents session fixation attacks.
The php_sapi_name() function returns the Server API name, such as 'cli' for command-line interface.

session_destroy() destroys all data associated with the current session on the server, but it does not remove the session cookie from the user's browser; that must be done manually (e.g., with setcookie()).
In PHP, you must call session_start() before $_SESSION is populated with session data; without it, $_SESSION remains an empty array.
The array_find() function was introduced in PHP 8.3.
Property hooks were introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.4.
Asymmetric visibility for properties (e.g., `public private(set)`) was introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing different access levels for reading and writing a property.
The #[NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.3.
The pipe operator |> has been proposed in multiple RFCs for PHP but has never been implemented in any released version.
The clone-with syntax was introduced in PHP 8.3 as part of an RFC that allows overriding properties during cloning.
array_first() and array_last() do not exist in any version of PHP; they were proposed as RFCs for PHP 8.1 but were never introduced.
The RFC Partial Function Application v2 was adopted for PHP 9.0, the major release expected around November 2026.
The PHP clamp_v2 RFC implementing the clamp() function was accepted and released in PHP 8.3.
The Context Managers v2 RFC was accepted and shipped in PHP 8.5, which was released in November 2025, so as of 2026-11-07 it has been adopted.
The RFC for Bound-Erased Generic Types was indeed proposed and ultimately declined in the PHP internals community.
The RFC to make ZTS (Zend Thread Safety) the default has not been accepted in PHP; as of PHP 8.3/8.4, non-thread-safe builds remain the default.
As of PHP 8.5 (which is still in development), generics have not been implemented, despite being a long-discussed and targeted feature.
Based on PHP's annual November release pattern, PHP 8.5 would be the latest stable version as of 2026-11-07, with PHP 8.6 scheduled for GA on 2026-11-19.
PHP 6 was an abandoned branch intended to add Unicode support, and after PHP 5.6 the next release was indeed PHP 7.0.
The RFC for the #[\Deprecated] attribute was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.4, allowing developers to mark functions/methods as deprecated directly via attributes.
In both Clean Architecture and Onion Architecture, the dependency rule mandates that all source code dependencies point inward toward the core, meaning inner layers have no knowledge of outer layers.

According to clean architecture and DDD principles, domain entities should remain framework-agnostic, depending only on PHP itself (and possibly the standard library), with no imports from Doctrine or Symfony.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation layer, not the business-logic layer, even though controllers call use cases.
The onion architecture places the Domain Model (entities) at its very center, with all other layers (Domain Services, Application Services, UI) built outward around it.

Deptrac (and similar tools like phparkitect) statically analyze code to detect forbidden dependencies between architectural layers and will report a failure when a class violates a defined layer rule.

Use cases must be independent of external frameworks; accepting HTTP requests or EntityManager directly violates the dependency rule of Clean Architecture by coupling business logic to delivery and persistence layers.
In Domain-Driven Design, a Repository provides a collection-like interface for aggregates/entities while hiding the persistence/storage mechanism behind an abstraction.
In clean architecture, the database is part of the infrastructure/outer layer, and the dependency rule ensures domain and use-case layers are independent of it.
An aggregate is a cluster of domain entities and value objects treated as a single unit for consistency, not a database table.
Value Objects are defined by being immutable and compared by their attribute values rather than by a unique identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the single entry point through which all changes to an aggregate must go, ensuring consistency and integrity.
In DDD, repositories are responsible for managing aggregate roots only; entities within an aggregate are accessed through their root, not via separate repositories.
Ubiquitous language is a core concept of Domain-Driven Design, referring to a shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts that is embedded in the model.

In model theory, an elementary submodel is the boundary within which a model and its language remain consistent (satisfy the same first-order sentences), while in a larger model outside that boundary the same terms may denote different elements.
DDD recommends rich domain models where objects encapsulate both data and behavior; an anemic model is considered an anti-pattern.

In DDD, a bounded context defines the boundary within which a specific domain model applies, so the same concept in different bounded contexts is represented as a different class with its own meaning.
In Symfony DI, services are NOT lazy by default; the `lazy: true` option must be explicitly set to defer instantiation until a method is actually called on the proxy.
The `debug:router` command lists all registered routes in a Symfony application.
Symfony autowiring automatically resolves and injects services based on constructor type hints, eliminating the need to manually declare every service in services.yaml.
Twig compiles templates into PHP classes and caches the compiled code between requests to improve performance.
In Symfony's dev environment, the container is cached and only recompiled when one of its tracked configuration files changes (via a freshness check comparing file metadata).
The APP_ENV environment variable determines the active Symfony environment (e.g., dev, prod, test).
Symfony requires controller methods to be public; private methods cannot be called by the routing framework.

Event subscribers do not automatically receive events before listeners; execution order depends solely on the priority value assigned to each listener, regardless of whether it was registered via a subscriber or directly.
Symfony 6.0 removed the old Guard system entirely, leaving only the new authenticator system based on AuthenticatorInterface.
The #[IsGranted('ROLE_X')] attribute checks if the user has a role or permission and throws an AccessDeniedHttpException (403) if they don't.
Symfony Voters are indeed the mechanism for checking access to specific objects, using isGranted() with an attribute and a subject/object.
Symfony 7 removed support for doctrine annotations; validation constraints must now be declared as PHP attributes.
In Symfony, the `csrf_protection` option defaults to `true`, meaning forms automatically validate the CSRF token on submission unless explicitly disabled.
Symfony always performs server-side validation regardless of client-side HTML5 validation results, ensuring security and data integrity.
The Symfony MakerBundle command `make:form` generates a FormType class with a corresponding form type.
Symfony stores the password hash (not the plain text password) in the session to verify that the user's credentials have not changed during the session.
With Symfony Flex, bundle and service configurations are stored as individual YAML/PHP files in the config/packages/ directory, one per bundle or topic.
In Symfony, the .env file is committed to the repository with dev defaults, while .env.local (gitignored) holds real secrets and overrides.
The `debug:container` Symfony command lists all registered services and their aliases in the dependency injection container.

The compiled Symfony container does not expose a setParameter() method; parameters are immutable once the container is compiled and the setParameter() method only exists on ContainerBuilder during the compilation phase.
By default, Symfony services are private (public: false); you cannot fetch them directly from the container anymore.
In Symfony, configuration is optional for most bundles; they work out of the box with default settings defined in their extension class.
In Symfony, environment variables are referenced in services.yaml using the %env(VAR)% syntax, e.g., %env(DB_HOST)%.
The APP_DEBUG environment variable enables debug mode in Symfony, activating the Web Profiler and Twig debugging features.
A single message in Symfony Messenger can have multiple handlers, each performing different actions (e.g., persisting to DB, sending notifications) for the same message.
Sync transport handles the message immediately within the same request/response cycle, without queuing it for a worker; only async transport queues messages for workers.
The Symfony console command `messenger:consume` starts a worker that consumes messages from a transport (queue) via the Messenger component.
In Symfony Messenger, retry_strategy can be configured per transport via transport options (as a default), though individual messages can override it via attributes.
Symfony Messenger uses the Symfony Serializer component by default, which serializes messages to JSON format for transport.
The Symfony Scheduler component creates messages (like RunTaskMessage) on a defined schedule and dispatches them through Symfony Messenger's bus for processing.
Symfony's Messenger component provides a built-in 'doctrine' transport that stores messages in database tables via Doctrine DBAL, using a DSN like doctrine://default.
Symfony Messenger uses a middleware stack and allows adding custom middleware in the bus configuration, which can be placed before or after the built-in middleware.

Symfony has historically followed a schedule of major releases every two years and minor releases every six months (typically around May and November), which is the widely cited release cadence in Symfony documentation and educational materials.
Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.3 as its minimum version, following the pattern of bumping the PHP requirement with each major release.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations in favor of PHP 8 attributes, dropping the dependency on doctrine/annotations.
Symfony's AssetMapper component manages CSS/JS assets without Node.js or webpack by using an importmap.php file to define module mappings.
Symfony 6.4 is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release, not a regular release; Symfony releases LTS versions every two years (2.8, 3.4, 4.4, 5.4, 6.4, 7.4, etc.).
Symfony's policy is that deprecations from the previous major version are removed in the next major release.
Symfony provides an UPGRADE.md guide for each major release listing changes, deprecations, and upgrade steps.
Symfony's AssetMapper component (symfony/asset-mapper) manages front-end assets and importmap directly without requiring Node.js or Webpack.

Based on Symfony's historical release cadence, November minor releases (e.g., 7.2 was November 20, 2024) typically occur around mid-to-late November, so 8.2 would likely not yet be released by November 7, 2026.
Following Symfony's six-month release cycle (x.0 in Nov, x.1 in May, x.2 in Nov), Symfony 8.2 is indeed expected in November 2026.
Symfony follows semantic versioning, so after 8.1 the next minor release is 8.2.
Symfony 8.x does not exist (current major version is 7.x), and even if it did, a .2 version would be a minor release that is backward-compatible, not a major release requiring rewrites.

Within the same major version (e.g., 8.1 → 8.2), PHP guarantees backward compatibility; only deprecated features emit warnings, not errors, and no code changes are required for minor version upgrades.
Symfony follows a pattern of releasing 4 minor versions per major cycle (e.g., 7.0 through 7.4 before 8.0), so the last minor version of 8.x before Symfony 9.0 is 8.4.
Symfony 8.2 is expected to require PHP 8.3 or 8.4, not 8.5, as Symfony typically doesn't require the very latest PHP version and PHP 8.5 would be too new at that point.

Symfony's deprecation policy states that deprecations introduced in a minor version of a major release are not removed until the next major version, so 8.x deprecations would not be removed before 9.0.

Twig does not allow arbitrary PHP code execution inside {{ }}; it only permits a restricted set of functions, filters, and object method calls as defined by the template environment and security policies.
Twig auto-escapes printed variables by default using HTML escaping unless the |raw filter is applied or autoescaping is explicitly disabled.
In Twig, the |e (short for |escape) filter escapes a string by converting special characters to HTML entities, making it safe for output in an HTML context.
The `format_number` filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number according to a specified locale.
In Twig, the |raw filter marks a value as safe, preventing it from being auto-escaped when rendered.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs an expression value and {% %} is used for tags like conditions, loops, and set statements.
Twig allows declaring variables inside templates using the `set` tag, e.g. `{% set name = 'World' %}`.
The Twig dump() function displays the debug structure of a variable, such as arrays and objects.
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JS library providing pre-built UI components and responsive design, not a single-page application framework like React, Angular, or Vue.
The .container class in Bootstrap provides a responsive fixed-width container whose max-width is set per breakpoint (e.g., 540px, 720px, 960px, 1140px).
Bootstrap's grid splits a row into 12 columns, not 16, and while older versions used floats, Bootstrap 4+ uses Flexbox.
Bootstrap 5 defines 6 breakpoints (xs, sm, md, lg, xl, xxl), but 'xs' has no infix in class names (it's the default), leaving sm, md, lg, xl, xxl as the five named breakpoints that appear as infixes.
Bootstrap spacing utilities use a scale where each number is a multiple of the $spacer variable (default 1rem), e.g., .mt-3 = 3 * $spacer.
In Bootstrap 5, the data-bs-toggle attribute is used to enable interactive components such as dropdowns, modals, and tabs on an element.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency and reimplemented all components using vanilla JavaScript.
Dark mode in Bootstrap 5.3+ is enabled by adding the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the <html> element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM does not automatically create tables at runtime; schema creation must be done explicitly via the SchemaTool, the doctrine:schema:create CLI command, or migrations.
The persist() method on EntityManager marks a new object as managed and schedules an INSERT to be executed only when flush() is called.
In Doctrine ORM 3, the merge() method was removed entirely (it was deprecated in 2.x); additionally, even when it existed, it returned a new managed copy rather than making the passed object managed.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) is written in terms of entity classes and their mapped fields, not the underlying database tables and columns.
Doctrine's EntityRepository::find() method returns null when no entity with the given identifier exists.
DoctrineBundle does not automatically call flush() at the end of every request; the developer must explicitly call $entityManager->flush() to persist changes.
In Doctrine ORM, once an entity is in the MANAGED state, the Unit of Work automatically detects property changes and generates UPDATE statements on flush() without needing another persist() call.
Doctrine's remove() only marks the entity for deletion in the Unit of Work; the actual SQL DELETE is executed during flush().
MVCC is specifically designed so that readers do NOT block writers and writers do NOT block readers, which is its main advantage over lock-based concurrency control.
The EXPLAIN command (and its synonym DESCRIBE in MySQL) displays the execution plan for a query without actually running it.

PostgreSQL treats each NULL as distinct, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL in the column.
string_agg() is the PostgreSQL aggregate function that concatenates non-null string values with a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM marks dead tuple space as reusable within the same table but does not return it to the operating system; only VACUUM FULL shrinks the file and releases space to the OS.
The PARTITION BY clause in a window function definition divides rows into groups over which the function is computed.
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but does NOT prevent non-repeatable reads; protecting against non-repeatable reads requires the REPEATABLE READ isolation level.
PostgreSQL's default mode is autocommit, where each individual SQL statement is treated as a transaction and automatically committed upon completion.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all changes made during that transaction.
Indexes benefit UPDATE and DELETE operations as well, because they allow the database engine to quickly locate the rows matching the WHERE clause instead of scanning the entire table.
PostgreSQL uses SAVEPOINT to create named rollback points within a transaction, allowing partial rollback of statements.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and then shows the plan with runtime statistics, whereas plain EXPLAIN shows the plan without executing.
pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension that adds vector data types and indexing support for efficient embedding similarity search.
A partial index in PostgreSQL is created with a WHERE clause and only indexes rows that satisfy that condition.

PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), an optimistic approach that tracks read/write dependencies and aborts conflicting transactions, rather than locking rows.
HTTP status code 201 Created indicates that the request has been fulfilled and a new resource has been successfully created.
HTTP status code 204 No Content indicates the request was successful but there is no content to return in the response body, commonly seen after DELETE operations.
RFC 7231 defines DELETE as idempotent because multiple identical DELETE requests have the same effect on the server as a single request.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is sent by the server in its response, not by the client; it indicates which origins the server permits to access the resource.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests is the standard status code returned when a client has exceeded a rate limit, as defined in RFC 6585.
It's the opposite: 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type HTTP header indicates the MIME type (media type) of the data in the request or response body.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that PATCH is not necessarily idempotent, whereas PUT is defined as idempotent in RFC 7231/9110.
Plain == is vulnerable to timing attacks; use hash_equals() for constant-time comparison of password hashes.

The Content-Security-Policy HTTP header enables the CSP policy, allowing server operators to define trusted sources of content for the browser to load.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol; the access token grants resource access but does not inherently identify the user (that role belongs to OpenID Connect built on top of it).
XSS is primarily prevented by proper context-aware output encoding/escaping when rendering data to HTML, not by server-side input validation before storing it in the database.
In the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, the 'code' parameter (authorization code) is returned to the redirect_uri and subsequently exchanged for an access token at the token endpoint.
A refresh token is specifically designed to have a longer lifetime than an access token and is used to obtain new access tokens without re-prompting the user for credentials.
A salt is not a secret; it is stored alongside the hash and is needed publicly for verification, unlike a pepper which must be kept secret.
PHPUnit only runs test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase; the test runner uses reflection and checks for that inheritance.
setUp() runs before each individual test, not once before all tests; setUpBeforeClass() is the one that runs once before all tests of the class.
A data provider can supply multiple sets of arguments, causing the test to run once per set; it is not limited to exactly one.
The `expectException()` method in PHPUnit declares that an exception of a given class (and optionally a given message) is expected to be thrown during the test.
It's the opposite: a stub only returns data, while a mock verifies which methods were called.
PHPUnit 10 introduced attributes like #[DataProvider] as the recommended way to supply test data, deprecating the older @dataProvider annotation.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, which also allows the return value of the depended-upon test to be passed as an argument to the depending test.
The --order-by=random option (or the shorthand --random-order) makes PHPUnit run tests in random order.
